en: An octopus has three hearts. Two of them pump blood to the gills, and the third pumps it to the rest of the body. And its blood is blue, because it uses copper instead of iron to carry oxygen.
About two thirds of an octopus's brain cells are not in its head, but in its arms. Each arm can react on its own, and the suckers can actually taste whatever they touch.
Octopuses can change the color and even the texture of their skin in a fraction of a second to disappear into the background. And the craziest part: scientists believe most octopuses are colorblind.
Octopuses are amazing escape artists. Because they have no bones, a big octopus can squeeze its whole body through a hole barely bigger than its beak, the only hard part of its body.

hook.en: Octopuses are masters of disguise, yet they're colorblind.

en: The Moon is slowly running away from us. Every year it moves about three point eight centimeters farther from Earth, roughly as fast as your fingernails grow.
The footprints left by the Apollo astronauts are probably still there today. With no wind and no rain on the Moon, they could stay almost untouched for millions of years.
We always see the same side of the Moon. It spins exactly once each time it goes around the Earth, so one whole side of it is never visible from here.
The Moon has moonquakes. Because the Moon is so dry and rigid, some of them can make the ground shake for more than ten minutes, much longer than most earthquakes on Earth.

hook.en: There's a side of the Moon we never see.

en: The Aztecs and the Maya used cocoa beans as money. With a handful of beans you could buy food at the market, so for them, chocolate really did grow on trees.
Chocolate is poisonous to dogs. It contains a substance called theobromine that humans digest easily, but dogs process it so slowly that even a small amount of dark chocolate can make them very sick.
White chocolate is not really chocolate. It contains no cocoa solids at all, only cocoa butter, sugar and milk. That's why it doesn't taste anything like dark chocolate.
For thousands of years, chocolate was only a drink, often bitter and spicy. The first solid chocolate bars were only made in England in the eighteen forties.

hook.en: White chocolate isn't really chocolate.

en: Your brain contains around eighty six billion nerve cells, called neurons. Each one can connect to thousands of others, creating more connections than there are stars in our galaxy.
Your brain is only about two percent of your body weight, but it uses around twenty percent of all your energy. Thinking is hard work, even when you are resting.
The brain itself cannot feel pain. It has no pain sensors, which is why surgeons can operate on some patients' brains while they are wide awake and talking.
Your brain is about sixty percent fat, which makes it one of the fattiest organs in your body. That's one reason healthy fats in your food are so important for it.

hook.en: Your brain can't feel any pain.

en: The pyramids were probably not built by slaves. Archaeologists found the villages, bakeries and tombs of paid workers who were proud of their job, and some of them even wrote their team names on the stones.
Ancient Egyptians created a calendar with three hundred sixty five days, divided into twelve months. It's one of the ancestors of the calendar we still use today.
In ancient Egypt, both men and women wore dark eye makeup. It looked great, but it also helped reduce the glare of the desert sun, and it may even have helped fight eye infections.
Egyptians adored their cats. According to the Greek historian Herodotus, when a family cat died, the people of the house shaved off their eyebrows as a sign of mourning.

hook.en: Ancient Egyptian men wore eye makeup too.

en: A bolt of lightning is about five times hotter than the surface of the Sun. It can reach around thirty thousand degrees Celsius, for just a fraction of a second.
Lightning strikes somewhere on Earth around forty to fifty times every single second. That's more than a billion flashes every year.
Lightning can definitely strike the same place twice. The Empire State Building in New York is hit around twenty times every year, which is exactly why tall buildings have lightning rods.

Thunder is the sound of air exploding. Lightning heats the air so fast that it expands violently. Count the seconds between the flash and the thunder, divide by three, and you get the distance of the storm in kilometers.

hook.en: Lightning does strike the same place twice.

en: Emperor penguins are amazing divers. They can go deeper than five hundred meters and hold their breath for more than twenty minutes while hunting for fish. That's deeper than one and a half Eiffel Towers stacked on top of each other.
Male emperor penguins keep their egg warm on their feet for about two months, in the middle of the Antarctic winter, without eating anything at all.
Penguins can drink salt water. A special gland above their eyes filters the salt out of their blood, and they simply sneeze it out.
Not all penguins live in the cold. The Galapagos penguin lives right near the equator, and in South Africa, penguins waddle on sunny beaches next to tourists.

hook.en: Penguins can drink salt water.

en: Corals look like rocks or plants, but they are actually animals. They are tiny creatures related to jellyfish, living together in huge colonies.
Coral reefs cover less than one percent of the ocean floor, but around a quarter of all ocean species depend on them at some point in their lives.
The Great Barrier Reef in Australia is the largest structure built by living things on the planet. It's so big that it can be seen from space.
Parrotfish eat coral and poop out fine white sand. A single large parrotfish can produce hundreds of kilograms of sand every year, and many tropical beaches are partly made of it.

hook.en: Tiny animals built something you can see from space.

en: Mount Everest is still growing. The Indian plate keeps pushing into Asia, lifting the mountain by a few millimeters every year.
The top of Everest was once at the bottom of the sea. Climbers walk on rock that contains fossils of tiny sea creatures that lived hundreds of millions of years ago.
At the summit, each breath gives you only about a third of the oxygen you would get at sea level. That's why most climbers carry oxygen bottles to reach the top.
Everest is the highest mountain above sea level, but not the tallest. Mauna Kea in Hawaii is more than ten thousand meters tall if you measure it from its base on the ocean floor.

hook.en: Everest's summit has only a third of the oxygen.

en: Your heart beats about one hundred thousand times every day. Over a whole life, that's more than two and a half billion beats, without ever taking a break.
Every day, your heart pumps around seven thousand liters of blood through your body. That's enough to fill a small tanker truck.
Your heart has its own electrical system. It doesn't need your brain to tell it when to beat, and it can even keep beating for a short time outside the body.
The biggest heart on the planet belongs to the blue whale. It weighs around one hundred and eighty kilograms, about as much as two adult humans, and it can beat as slowly as twice a minute.

hook.en: Your heart can beat without your brain.

en: Cats cannot taste sweet things. They are missing the gene that makes sweet taste receptors, so a cake means nothing special to them.
Adult cats almost never meow at each other. They mostly meow to talk to humans, so in a way, they invented a language just for us.
Cats sleep between twelve and sixteen hours a day. That means a nine year old cat has spent around five years of its life asleep, more than half of its whole life.
Cats have a special organ in the roof of their mouth that lets them taste smells. When a cat sniffs something with its mouth slightly open and a funny face, it's using that organ.

hook.en: Your cat spends most of its life asleep.

en: Mars has the tallest volcano in the solar system. It's called Olympus Mons, and it's about two and a half times taller than Mount Everest.
Sunsets on Mars are blue. The fine dust in the Martian air scatters blue light around the Sun, the opposite of what happens on Earth. NASA rovers have photographed these blue sunsets many times.
Mars is red because it's rusty. Its rocks and dust are full of iron oxide, the same thing that makes old metal turn red.
Mars has two tiny moons, Phobos and Deimos. Phobos is slowly spiraling closer, and in about fifty million years it will either crash into Mars or break apart into a ring.

hook.en: Mars is red because it's rusty.

en: Legend says coffee was discovered by a goat herder in Ethiopia called Kaldi. He noticed his goats became super energetic after eating red berries from a certain bush.
Coffee beans are not really beans. They are the seeds of a small red fruit called a coffee cherry, and most cherries hold two seeds pressed together, flat side to flat side.
The country that drinks the most coffee per person is not Italy or America, it's Finland. The average Finn drinks around four cups a day.
Coffee was once banned in several places. In the sixteen hundreds, some rulers believed coffee houses were places where people gathered to criticize them and plot against them.

hook.en: The world's biggest coffee drinkers aren't Italian.

en: Vikings never wore horned helmets in battle. That famous image was invented in the eighteen hundreds by costume designers for operas.

Vikings reached North America around the year one thousand, almost five hundred years before Christopher Columbus. The remains of their camp were found in Canada. The site, called L'Anse aux Meadows, is on the island of Newfoundland.
Vikings were actually quite clean. Combs are one of the most common things archaeologists find, and in old Norse, Saturday was named washing day.
Some historians think Vikings navigated with a special crystal called a sunstone. By looking at the sky through it, they could find the position of the Sun, even on cloudy days.

hook.en: Vikings were much cleaner than you think.

en: There are around thirteen hundred potentially active volcanoes on land, but most volcanic activity on Earth actually happens hidden under the oceans, along huge underwater mountain chains.
Lava can reach about twelve hundred degrees Celsius. That's hot enough to melt many types of metal, and some very runny lava flows can move faster than a person can run.
In eighteen eighty three, the eruption of Krakatoa in Indonesia made what may be the loudest sound in recorded history. People heard it almost five thousand kilometers away.
Lightning can strike inside volcanic ash clouds. The tiny pieces of ash rub against each other and create static electricity, producing a terrifying show called a dirty thunderstorm.

hook.en: A volcano made the loudest sound in history.

en: Dolphins sleep with only half of their brain at a time. The other half stays awake to keep breathing and to watch for danger.

Each dolphin has its own signature whistle, a bit like a name. Other dolphins use that whistle to call it. Scientists found that dolphins can remember the whistles of old companions for more than twenty years.
Dolphins can recognize themselves in a mirror. Only a few animals can do that, like great apes, elephants and magpies.
Some dolphins in Australia use sea sponges as tools. They wear them on their noses to protect themselves while digging for food on the rough sea floor, and mothers teach this trick to their babies.

hook.en: Dolphins can recognize themselves in a mirror.

en: Most of the deep ocean has never been seen by human eyes. We have better maps of the surface of Mars than of our own sea floor.
Below about one thousand meters, the ocean is completely dark. Scientists call it the midnight zone, and no sunlight ever reaches it.
Around three quarters of the animals living in the deep sea can make their own light. They use it to hunt, to hide, and to find a partner.
The colossal squid lives in the deep sea and has the biggest eyes in the animal kingdom. Each eye can be as large as a dinner plate, perfect for spotting faint light in the dark.

hook.en: Most deep sea animals make their own light.

en: The Eiffel Tower grows in summer. When the iron heats up it expands, and the tower can get up to fifteen centimeters taller.
The tower was supposed to be temporary. It was built for the eighteen eighty nine World's Fair, and it was saved partly because it was useful as a giant radio antenna.
The Eiffel Tower is repainted about every seven years, by hand, with brushes. Each time it takes around sixty tonnes of paint, and the work lasts more than a year.
There is a secret apartment at the top of the Eiffel Tower. Gustave Eiffel built it for himself, and he welcomed famous guests there, like the inventor Thomas Edison.

hook.en: The Eiffel Tower is still painted by hand.

en: You spend about one third of your life asleep. If you live to ninety, that's around thirty years of sleeping.
During dream sleep, your body is almost completely paralyzed. It's a protection, so you don't act out your dreams and run around the room.
In nineteen sixty four, a student named Randy Gardner stayed awake for about eleven days. By the end, he had trouble focusing, remembering things, and even saw things that weren't there.
Some animals sleep in very strange ways. Sperm whales sleep vertically, floating in the ocean like giant logs, during short naps of around ten to fifteen minutes.

hook.en: A student once stayed awake for eleven days.

en: Honey never goes bad. Archaeologists found pots of honey in ancient Egyptian tombs, thousands of years old, and it was still edible.
A single honeybee makes only about one twelfth of a teaspoon of honey in its whole life. Every jar is the work of thousands of bees.

Bees tell each other where to find flowers by dancing. The angle and the length of their waggle dance show the direction and the distance. The scientist who decoded this dance, Karl von Frisch, won a Nobel Prize for it.
To make just one kilogram of honey, bees must visit around four million flowers and fly a distance equal to roughly three or four trips around the Earth.

hook.en: Bees give each other directions by dancing.

en: The Sun is so big that around one point three million Earths could fit inside it. And yet, compared to the other stars in the universe, it is only an average size star.
Sunlight takes about eight minutes and twenty seconds to reach us. So when you look at the Sun, you are seeing it as it was eight minutes ago.
The Sun contains about ninety nine point eight percent of all the mass in our solar system. All the planets together are just leftovers.
The Sun is not actually yellow, it's white. It only looks yellow from the ground because our atmosphere scatters part of its blue light. Astronauts in space see it as white.

hook.en: The Sun is almost the entire solar system.

en: Botanically speaking, a banana is a berry, but a strawberry is not. A true berry grows from a single flower with one ovary.
Bananas are slightly radioactive. They contain potassium, and a tiny part of it is naturally radioactive. Don't worry, you would need to eat millions at once for it to matter.
Banana plants are not trees. They have no wood at all. They are actually giant herbs, some of the biggest on the planet. What looks like a trunk is actually made of leaves rolled tightly together.

Almost all the bananas we eat today are clones of a single variety called the Cavendish. Before the nineteen fifties, people ate a different banana, the Gros Michel, until a disease almost wiped it out.

hook.en: Banana plants aren't trees at all.

en: Ancient Romans used urine to wash their clothes. The ammonia in it helped remove stains, and some laundries collected it from public pots in the street.
Roman concrete has survived for two thousand years. Some of it, in harbors, even got stronger over time thanks to sea water.
At its peak, the Roman Empire ruled around sixty million people. That may have been up to a quarter of everyone alive on Earth at the time.
Romans had public toilets with long stone benches where people sat side by side and chatted. Instead of toilet paper, they used a sea sponge on a stick, which may have been shared.

hook.en: Rome may have ruled a quarter of humanity.

en: The very first airplane flight, by the Wright brothers in nineteen oh three, lasted just twelve seconds. It flew a shorter distance than the wingspan of a modern jumbo jet.
Food tastes blander on airplanes. The dry air and the low cabin pressure reduce your sense of taste for salty and sweet things by around a third.
On average, every passenger plane is struck by lightning about once a year. They are built for it, and the electricity flows around the outside of the plane.
The famous black box on an airplane is not black at all. It's bright orange, so that rescue teams can find it more easily after an accident.

hook.en: Every plane gets hit by lightning about once a year.

en: Elephants are one of the very few mammals that cannot jump. Their legs are built to carry their huge weight, not to lift it off the ground.
An elephant's trunk has tens of thousands of muscles. It's strong enough to pull down a tree, and precise enough to pick up a single peanut.
Elephants can communicate with very deep rumbles that humans can't hear. Other elephants can feel these vibrations through their feet, kilometers away.
Elephants seem to recognize their dead. When they find the bones of another elephant, they often stop, touch them gently with their trunks and feet, and stay there for a while in silence.

hook.en: Elephants can hear through their feet.

en: The United States gets more tornadoes than any other country, more than a thousand every year. Most of them hit a region in the middle of the country nicknamed Tornado Alley.
The fastest wind ever measured on Earth was inside a tornado in Oklahoma in nineteen ninety nine. Radar recorded it at around four hundred eighty kilometers per hour, faster than a Formula One car.
Tornadoes have been seen on every continent except Antarctica. Over water, they are called waterspouts, and they can suck up water, and sometimes even fish and frogs.
Some tornadoes are almost invisible. A tornado only becomes visible when it picks up dust and debris, or when water droplets condense into a funnel shaped cloud.

hook.en: Tornadoes can suck up fish and frogs.

en: Sharks are older than trees. The first sharks swam in the oceans more than four hundred million years ago, while the first real trees appeared millions of years later.
Sharks don't have a single bone in their body. Their skeleton is made of cartilage, the same flexible material you have in your nose and ears.
The Greenland shark may be the longest living animal with a backbone. Scientists estimate some of them are around four hundred years old, and they only become adults at about one hundred fifty.
Sharks have a sixth sense. Tiny pores on their snout detect the weak electric fields made by the muscles of other animals, even fish hiding under the sand.

hook.en: Some sharks alive today were born centuries ago.

en: After hitting the iceberg, the Titanic sank in about two hours and forty minutes. Of the roughly twenty two hundred people on board, more than fifteen hundred died.
The Titanic only had lifeboats for about half of the people on board. Shockingly, that was still more than the law required at the time.
The wreck was only found in nineteen eighty five, almost four kilometers deep. Today, bacteria are slowly eating the metal, and parts of the ship could collapse within a few decades.
One of the Titanic's bakers, Charles Joughin, survived for hours in the freezing water. He said he had been drinking whisky that night, and he lived to the age of seventy eight.

hook.en: Bacteria are eating the Titanic right now.

en: The image that lands at the back of your eye is upside down. Your brain flips it automatically, so you never notice.
Humans can tell apart around one million different colors. Some people, almost always women, may even see many more thanks to an extra type of color cell.
You blink around fifteen to twenty times every minute. That adds up to several minutes with your eyes closed every hour you are awake.
Each of your eyes has a blind spot, where the nerve leaves the eye to go to the brain. You never notice it, because your brain simply fills in the missing part of the picture.

hook.en: You spend minutes every hour with your eyes closed.

en: Saturn could float in water. It's the only planet in our solar system that is less dense than water, because it's mostly made of light gases.
Saturn's rings are almost three hundred thousand kilometers wide, but in most places they are only about ten meters thick. They are made of pieces of ice and rock.
Saturn has more than two hundred seventy known moons, more than any other planet. One of them, Titan, has lakes and rivers, not of water, but of liquid methane.
It may rain diamonds on Saturn. Scientists think lightning turns methane into soot, which gets squeezed into diamonds as it falls deeper and deeper into the planet.

hook.en: Saturn has a moon with lakes that aren't water.

en: The story goes that the Margherita pizza was named after Queen Margherita of Italy in eighteen eighty nine. Its colors, red, white and green, match the Italian flag.
Hawaiian pizza, with pineapple, wasn't invented in Hawaii. It was created in Canada in nineteen sixty two by a Greek immigrant named Sam Panopoulos.
In twenty seventeen, UNESCO added the art of the Neapolitan pizza maker to its list of the cultural heritage of humanity, next to traditions that are centuries old.
Pizza started as cheap street food for poor workers in Naples. People bought it from street sellers and ate it folded in half, long before it became a worldwide favorite.

hook.en: Pizza making is officially world heritage.

en: The Amazon rainforest makes a lot of its own rain. Its trees release so much water vapor that they create huge flying rivers of moisture in the sky.
The Amazon is home to around one in ten of all the known species on Earth, and scientists keep discovering new ones every year.
Every year, millions of tonnes of dust from the Sahara desert fly across the Atlantic Ocean and fall on the Amazon, bringing nutrients that help the rainforest grow.
The Amazon River carries more water than the next seven biggest rivers in the world combined. And yet, there isn't a single bridge that crosses it.

hook.en: The Sahara desert feeds the Amazon rainforest.

en: Owls can turn their heads around two hundred seventy degrees. Special blood vessels in their neck keep blood flowing to the brain while they twist. That's three quarters of a full circle.
Owl eyes are not round balls like ours, they are shaped like tubes. They can't move them at all, which is why owls turn their whole head to look around.
Owls fly almost in complete silence. Their feathers have soft, comb like edges that break up the air, so their prey never hears them coming.
A group of owls is called a parliament. And many owls swallow small prey whole, then cough up a little ball of bones and fur called a pellet.

hook.en: Owls can fly in almost total silence.

en: About ninety percent of an iceberg is hidden under water. That's where the expression the tip of the iceberg comes from.
The ice in many icebergs is thousands of years old. When it melts, tiny bubbles of ancient air pop, making a fizzing sound that sailors call bergy seltzer.
One of the biggest icebergs ever recorded, called B fifteen, broke off Antarctica in the year two thousand. It was about the size of the island of Jamaica.
Some icebergs are bright blue, or even striped. Very old, dense ice absorbs red light and reflects blue, which makes it glow like a giant blue gem.

hook.en: One iceberg was as big as Jamaica.

en: Young sunflowers follow the Sun across the sky during the day and turn back to the east at night. Once they are fully grown, most of them stay facing east. Scientists found this is driven by an internal clock, a bit like ours.
A sunflower head is not one flower. It's made of up to two thousand tiny flowers packed together in a perfect spiral pattern.
After the Chernobyl nuclear disaster, sunflowers were planted on rafts on nearby ponds. Their roots helped pull radioactive particles out of the water.
The tallest sunflower ever recorded was more than nine meters tall. It was grown in Germany in twenty fourteen, taller than a three story house.

hook.en: Sunflowers helped clean up after Chernobyl.

en: The fastest animal on Earth is the peregrine falcon. When it dives to catch its prey, it can go faster than three hundred twenty kilometers per hour.
A cheetah can reach around one hundred kilometers per hour in just a few seconds. But it can only keep that speed for a short sprint, before it has to stop and cool down.
For its size, a tiny mite from California is one of the fastest runners ever measured. It covers more than three hundred times its body length every second.
Dragonflies are among the fastest insects in the world, reaching around fifty kilometers per hour. And they are deadly hunters, catching their prey in more than nine out of ten attempts.

hook.en: The fastest runner for its size is a tiny mite.

en: Every dog's nose print is unique, just like a human fingerprint. Some dog registries have even used nose prints to identify dogs.
A dog's sense of smell is somewhere between ten thousand and one hundred thousand times better than ours. Some dogs can even smell certain diseases in humans.
Smart dogs can learn the meaning of more than one hundred and fifty words, and some exceptional dogs have learned the names of over a thousand toys.
Dogs dream, just like us. Puppies and small dogs dream more often, and when a sleeping dog twitches its paws, it may be running after something in its dream.

hook.en: Some dogs know over a thousand words.

en: A black hole's gravity is so strong that nothing can escape it, not even light. That's why it looks completely black. Scientists can only spot them by watching what happens to the stars and gas around them.
If you fell into a black hole, the difference in gravity between your head and your feet would stretch you like a noodle. Scientists actually call this spaghettification.
There's a giant black hole at the center of our own galaxy. It's about four million times heavier than the Sun, and scientists published the first picture of it in twenty twenty two.
If the entire Earth was squeezed into a black hole, it would be smaller than a marble, only about two centimeters wide.

hook.en: A giant black hole sits at our galaxy's center.

en: The Great Pyramid of Giza was the tallest human made structure on Earth for about thirty eight hundred years. That record is longer than any other building in history.
When it was finished, the Great Pyramid was not yellow and rough. It was covered in smooth white limestone that shone brightly in the sunlight.
The Great Pyramid is made of around two point three million stone blocks. Some of them weigh more than two elephants.
The Great Pyramid is lined up almost perfectly with north, south, east and west. The error is only a tiny fraction of a degree, built more than four thousand five hundred years ago.

hook.en: Some pyramid blocks weigh more than two elephants.

en: Babies are born with around three hundred bones, but adults have only two hundred and six. As we grow, many of them fuse together.
The smallest bone in your body is in your ear. It's called the stirrup, and it's about the size of a grain of rice.
Your bones are alive. Old bone is constantly removed and replaced, so your skeleton renews itself completely roughly every ten years. That's also why a broken bone can heal and become strong again.
Your strongest bone is the thigh bone, the femur. It is also the longest bone in your body, about a quarter of your height, and it can support around thirty times your body weight.

hook.en: You get a brand new skeleton every ten years.

en: Strawberries are the only fruit that wears its seeds on the outside, around two hundred of them on each berry. And botanically, it isn't even a real berry.
Strawberries belong to the rose family, along with apples, cherries, peaches and even almonds. If you look closely at a strawberry flower, it really does look like a tiny white wild rose.
There is a museum dedicated only to strawberries. It's in Belgium, in the village of Wepion near the city of Namur, a place that has been famous for growing them for more than a century.
Gram for gram, strawberries contain more vitamin C than oranges. A handful of them can give you most of what you need for the whole day.

hook.en: There's a museum just for strawberries.

en: Snow is not actually white. Each ice crystal is clear, but snow looks white because all those crystals scatter the light in every direction.
Snowflakes almost always have six sides. It's because of the way water molecules link together when they freeze, and the exact shape depends on the temperature and humidity inside the cloud.
According to records, the largest snowflakes ever reported fell in Montana in eighteen eighty seven. Witnesses said some were thirty eight centimeters wide, bigger than a pizza.
Snow can be pink or red. A type of algae that lives in snow turns it red in summer, and people call it watermelon snow, though you definitely shouldn't eat it.

hook.en: Snowflakes once fell as big as a pizza.

en: Butterflies taste with their feet. When they land on a leaf, sensors on their legs instantly tell them if it's a good place to lay their eggs.
Monarch butterflies migrate up to four thousand eight hundred kilometers, from Canada to Mexico. None of them has ever made the trip before.
A butterfly's colors come from thousands of tiny scales on its wings. Some of them have no pigment at all, and create color only by reflecting light.
Butterflies can't fly if they are too cold. They need their flight muscles to be warm, so you will often see them resting in the sun with their wings open to heat up.

hook.en: Some butterfly colors have no pigment at all.

en: Contrary to the famous myth, you can't see the Great Wall of China from the Moon. Even from low orbit, it's very hard to spot with the naked eye.
If you add up all of its sections, the Great Wall is more than twenty thousand kilometers long. That's about half the distance around the Earth.
Some sections of the wall were built with a mortar made of sticky rice mixed with lime. It made the wall incredibly strong, and some of it still stands today.
Building the Great Wall took more than two thousand years, across many different dynasties. So many workers died during its construction that it's sometimes called the longest cemetery on Earth.

hook.en: The Great Wall was built with sticky rice.

en: Antarctica is the largest desert in the world. A desert is about how little rain or snow falls, not about heat, and Antarctica gets very little.
The Antarctic ice sheet holds around seventy percent of all the fresh water on Earth. If it all melted, sea levels would rise by about fifty eight meters.
The coldest temperature ever measured on Earth was in Antarctica, in nineteen eighty three. It reached minus eighty nine point two degrees Celsius.
No one is born and raised in Antarctica. The only people living there are scientists and staff at research stations, around one thousand in winter and a few thousand in summer.

hook.en: Antarctica once hit minus eighty nine degrees.

en: The smartphone in your pocket is millions of times more powerful than the computer that guided Apollo eleven to the Moon in nineteen sixty nine. That old computer had less memory than a single photo on your phone.
The first smartphone was sold in nineteen ninety four. It was called the IBM Simon, it had a touch screen, and its battery lasted about one hour.
Today there are more mobile phone subscriptions in the world than there are people on Earth, more than eight billion. Many people simply have two phones, one for work and one for their private life.
Studies have found that a phone can carry more bacteria than a toilet seat. We touch them all day, then put them right next to our face.

hook.en: There are more phones than people on Earth.

en: Jellyfish have no brain, no heart, no blood and no bones. They are about ninety five percent water, and they sense the world with a simple net of nerves spread across their body.
There is a jellyfish that can turn back time. When it's hurt or old, the so called immortal jellyfish can turn itself back into a baby and start its life again.
Jellyfish were drifting through the oceans more than five hundred million years ago. That means they are older than dinosaurs, and even older than trees.
Some jellyfish glow in the dark. A glowing protein from one jellyfish became one of the most useful tools in biology, and its discovery won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in two thousand eight.

hook.en: Jellyfish are older than dinosaurs.

en: Jupiter's Great Red Spot is a storm bigger than the entire Earth, and astronomers have watched it rage for at least one hundred and ninety years.
Jupiter is the biggest planet, but it has the shortest day in the solar system. It spins around once in only about ten hours, so fast that it bulges out and looks slightly squashed.
Jupiter is so big that more than thirteen hundred Earths could fit inside it. It is more than twice as heavy as all the other planets of our solar system put together.
Jupiter has dozens of moons, and one of them, Ganymede, is the biggest moon in the solar system. It's even bigger than the planet Mercury.

hook.en: Over thirteen hundred Earths could fit inside Jupiter.

en: The oldest cheese ever found is about thirty six hundred years old. It was discovered on mummies buried in the desert of northwest China.
The holes in Swiss cheese come from bubbles of gas made by bacteria while the cheese ages. Tiny bits of hay in the milk help the bubbles form.
One of the most expensive cheeses in the world is made from donkey milk in Serbia. It can cost more than one thousand euros per kilo.
Some cheeses are made with the help of tiny mites. A French cheese called Mimolette gets its rough, cratered crust from cheese mites living on its surface.

hook.en: The priciest cheese comes from donkey milk.

en: Most of your dreams are forgotten within a few minutes of waking up. That's why many people believe they don't dream, even though everyone does. Writing your dream down right after waking up helps you remember it.
You have several dreams every night, mostly during a sleep stage called REM. Over a lifetime, you will spend around six years dreaming.
People who were born blind still dream. Their dreams are full of sounds, smells, touch and emotions instead of images.
In a lucid dream, you know that you are dreaming, and some people can even control what happens. Scientists have managed to exchange simple signals with people while they were lucid dreaming.

hook.en: People born blind still dream.

en: A rainbow is actually a full circle. From the ground, the horizon hides the bottom half, but pilots can sometimes see the whole ring from an airplane.
To see a rainbow, the Sun must always be behind you. The light enters raindrops in front of you, bounces inside them, and comes back toward your eyes.
In a double rainbow, the second rainbow has its colors in the opposite order. And no two people ever see exactly the same rainbow, because each one depends on where you stand.
Rainbows can also appear at night. On bright nights, the light of the full Moon can create a moonbow, although it usually looks white to our eyes.

hook.en: No two people ever see the same rainbow.

en: Kangaroos can't easily walk backwards. Their huge tail and powerful back legs are built for bouncing forward, and when they move slowly, they use their tail like a fifth leg.
A baby kangaroo, called a joey, is born the size of a jelly bean. It crawls into its mother's pouch and stays there for months.
Red kangaroos can cover around eight meters in a single jump, and they can hop at more than fifty kilometers per hour.
A kangaroo mother can feed two babies of different ages at once, and she produces two different types of milk at the same time, one for each baby.

hook.en: A kangaroo can jump eight meters in one leap.

en: Venice is built on more than one hundred small islands in a lagoon, connected by around four hundred bridges. Instead of streets, the city has about one hundred and fifty canals.
The city stands on millions of wooden poles driven deep into the mud. Without oxygen under water, the wood has lasted for centuries.
There are no cars in Venice. People get around on foot or by boat, and even the ambulances, the fire trucks and the mail delivery all travel on the water.
Venice is slowly sinking, and floods are becoming more common. Since twenty twenty, giant mobile barriers rise from the sea floor to protect the city from the highest tides.

hook.en: In Venice, even ambulances are boats.

en: The deepest point of the Mariana Trench is about eleven kilometers down. If you dropped Mount Everest into it, its peak would still be more than two kilometers under water.

At the bottom, the water pressure is more than one thousand times stronger than at the surface. Only specially built submarines can survive the trip. That's about eight tons pressing on every square inch.
Even there, humans have left their mark. A plastic bag was spotted at almost eleven kilometers deep, one of the deepest pieces of trash ever found.
Life still exists at the bottom. Scientists have found strange creatures like the Mariana snailfish, a small, almost see through fish living around eight thousand meters deep.

hook.en: We found plastic eleven kilometers under the sea.

en: Samurai usually carried two swords, a long one and a short one. Wearing the pair was a privilege reserved for the samurai class.
In the fifteen hundreds, there was an African samurai. His name was Yasuke, and he served one of the most powerful lords in Japan, Oda Nobunaga.

The samurai class was officially abolished in the eighteen seventies, as Japan modernized. Samurai even lost the right to carry their swords in public. Their last great stand was a rebellion in eighteen seventy seven.
Samurai armor was often made of small plates of iron or leather, tied together with silk cords. That made it light and flexible enough to ride and fight in.

hook.en: Samurai once lost the right to carry their swords.

en: Some types of bamboo can grow almost one meter in a single day. It's one of the fastest growing plants on the planet.
Bamboo looks like a tree, but it's actually a giant grass, a close cousin of the grass in your garden. A giant panda can eat between twelve and thirty eight kilograms of it every single day.
Some bamboo species flower only once every sixty to one hundred twenty years. Strangely, all the plants of that species flower at the same time around the world, and then die.
Bamboo is incredibly strong for its weight. In parts of Asia it's still used as scaffolding to build skyscrapers, tied together by skilled workers.

hook.en: Some bamboo only flowers once a century.

en: In the Oxford English Dictionary, the little word run has hundreds of different meanings. It's one of the most complicated words in the language.
Around one and a half billion people speak English, but most of them learned it as a second language. Only about four hundred million people grew up speaking it as their mother tongue.
The sentence the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog contains every letter of the alphabet. That's why it was used for decades to test typewriters and fonts.
English has borrowed words from hundreds of languages. Shampoo comes from Hindi, robot from Czech, and ketchup probably comes from a Chinese word for fish sauce.

hook.en: One famous sentence holds every letter of the alphabet.

en: A giraffe's neck has exactly the same number of bones as yours, seven. Each one is just much, much longer. In a giraffe, a single one of those neck bones can be more than twenty five centimeters long.
A giraffe's tongue is about half a meter long and dark purple. The dark color may protect it from sunburn while the giraffe eats all day.
Giraffes barely sleep. In the wild, they often rest for only a few minutes at a time, and sometimes less than two hours in a whole day.
A baby giraffe starts its life with a fall of almost two meters, because giraffe mothers give birth standing up. The baby can usually stand and walk within an hour.

hook.en: Giraffes barely sleep two hours a day.

en: The northern lights are caused by the Sun. Particles from the Sun hit gases high in our atmosphere, usually about one hundred kilometers or more above the ground, and make them glow.
The color depends on the gas and the height. Oxygen glows green or red, while nitrogen can make blue and purple lights, often along the bottom edge of the glowing curtain.
There are southern lights too, near Antarctica. And other planets have auroras as well, like Jupiter, where they are much bigger and more powerful than ours.
Sometimes the northern lights travel much farther south. In May twenty twenty four, a huge solar storm made them visible in places like Mexico and southern Europe.

hook.en: Other planets have northern lights too.

en: You are around thirty times more likely to laugh when you're with other people than when you're alone. Laughter is mostly a social signal.
Laughter is contagious. Just hearing someone laugh activates the parts of your brain that prepare your face to smile. That's one reason television shows used recorded laugh tracks for decades.

Rats laugh when they are tickled. Their laughter is too high pitched for us to hear, but special microphones can pick it up. In experiments, tickled rats even came back for more, chasing the hand that tickled them.
Real laughter and fake laughter are handled differently by the brain, and most people can tell the difference just by listening, even without seeing the person.

hook.en: Rats laugh when you tickle them.

en: Wombats are the only animals known to produce cube shaped droppings. Scientists found that the wall of their intestine has stiff parts and stretchy parts, which shape the dry waste into neat cubes as it moves along. Each wombat makes dozens of these little cubes every single night.

A wombat pouch opens toward the back, not the front. That is very clever for an animal that spends its life digging long burrows, because the baby inside is protected from flying dirt, sticks, and roots. Some wombat burrows are more than twenty meters long.

A wombat has a very tough rear end made mostly of cartilage. When a predator such as a dingo chases it, the wombat dives into its burrow and blocks the entrance with its bottom, which is hard to bite and almost impossible to pull out.

The closest living relative of the wombat is the koala. Long ago there were also giant wombat relatives. The biggest known one, called Phascolonus, probably weighed around two hundred kilograms, about as much as two big men, before it died out roughly forty thousand years ago.

hook.en: Wombats defend themselves with their butts.

en: Cleopatra was not Egyptian by family. She belonged to the Ptolemy dynasty, which came from Macedonian Greece, and her first language was Greek. According to the ancient writer Plutarch, she was the first ruler of her family in about three hundred years to learn the Egyptian language.

Cleopatra became queen at only eighteen years old. Following the custom of her family, she ruled together with her twelve year old younger brother, Ptolemy the thirteenth. But she did not want to share power, and soon the two of them were at war.

Cleopatra lived closer in time to us than to the building of the Great Pyramid. The pyramid was finished around twenty five hundred years before she died, but the first Moon landing happened only about two thousand years after her death. She truly belongs to a very late chapter of Egyptian history.

Cleopatra was the last active ruler of the Ptolemy dynasty, and her death in thirty before the common era ended the age of the pharaohs. After that, Egypt became a province of the Roman Empire, and it stayed under foreign rule for centuries.

hook.en: Cleopatra lived closer to us than to the pyramids.

en: An adult body holds about five liters of blood, roughly eight percent of your weight. More than half of it is a pale yellow liquid called plasma. The red color comes from the red blood cells floating in it, which carry oxygen around your body.

Your bone marrow makes about two million new red blood cells every single second. A red blood cell lives for around one hundred twenty days, so your body is constantly replacing old cells with fresh ones, and it never takes a break, not even while you sleep.

Blood inside your veins is never blue. It is always red, dark red when it carries little oxygen and bright red when it is full of oxygen. Veins only look blue through the skin because of the way light is absorbed and scattered by skin and tissue.

There is a blood type so rare that it is nicknamed golden blood. It is called Rh null, and it lacks a whole group of proteins found on other red blood cells. Only a few dozen people in the world have ever been found with it.

hook.en: Your blood is never blue.

en: Mercury is the smallest planet in our solar system, and it is also the closest to the Sun. It races around the Sun in just eighty eight Earth days, so a year on Mercury is shorter than three Earth months.

A day on Mercury is very strange. From one sunrise to the next takes about one hundred seventy six Earth days, which is twice as long as its year. That means on Mercury, a day lasts longer than a whole year.

Even though Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun, it has ice. Spacecraft data shows water ice hiding at its poles, inside deep craters where sunlight never reaches. Those dark crater floors stay far below freezing, while the sunlit side can reach about four hundred thirty degrees Celsius.

Mercury has an enormous iron core that makes up a big part of the planet. Scientists think the planet has been slowly shrinking for billions of years as that core cooled, and that its crust wrinkled into long cliffs, some taller than a mountain.

hook.en: The closest planet to the Sun has ice.

en: Deep under the streets of Paris lies a huge network of old stone quarry tunnels. Part of it holds the Catacombs, where the bones of an estimated six million people were moved, starting in the late seventeen eighties, because the city cemeteries were overflowing.

The oldest standing bridge across the river Seine in Paris is called the Pont Neuf, which means New Bridge. It was finished in sixteen oh seven, and the name stuck. It was also the first stone bridge in Paris built without houses along its sides.

In front of Notre Dame cathedral, a small bronze plaque on the ground marks point zero. Distances from Paris to other towns across France are measured from this very spot. So in a way, every road in France begins on that one little circle.

Long before it was called Paris, a Celtic tribe called the Parisii settled on an island in the Seine. The Romans later built a town there called Lutetia, and the city only took the name of the tribe much later.

hook.en: France measures its distances from one spot in Paris.

en: Water is one of the very few substances that gets lighter when it freezes. Ice is less dense than liquid water because water expands by about nine percent as it turns to ice. That is why ice floats, and why lakes freeze from the top down.

Water is the only common substance on Earth that exists naturally as a solid, a liquid, and a gas all at the same time. You can see ice, rivers, and invisible water vapor in the air, all around the same planet and often in the same place.

Our planet looks like a water world, because oceans cover about seventy one percent of its surface. But only around three percent of all that water is fresh, and most of the fresh water is locked away as ice in glaciers and ice sheets.

The water inside you is old. A grown person is roughly sixty percent water. Because water is constantly recycled by rain, rivers, and living things, scientists say some molecules you drink today were also drunk by animals living millions of years ago.

hook.en: Only three percent of Earth's water is fresh.

en: The oldest wooden wheel ever found was dug up in the Ljubljana Marshes in Slovenia in two thousand two. Scientists dated it to about five thousand one hundred fifty years ago. It was made from ash and oak wood, and it is still on display in a museum.

Boats are far older than wheels. A wooden canoe found in the Netherlands, called the Pesse canoe, is about ten thousand years old. So people were crossing water for thousands of years before anyone figured out how to roll a cart.

Great civilizations in the Americas, including the Aztecs and the Inca, never used wheeled vehicles for transport. Yet archaeologists have found little clay animal toys with wheels in Mexico, so people there understood the idea. They just had no large animals to pull carts.

The wheel itself was only half the invention. The hard part was the axle, because the wheel and the axle have to fit together tightly enough to turn smoothly. Scientists think early wheeled carts and the potter's wheel appeared in the same period, around five thousand years ago.

hook.en: The Aztecs used the wheel only for toys.

en: The Great Barrier Reef stretches for about two thousand three hundred kilometers along the northeast coast of Australia. Its total area is roughly the size of Italy, and it is not one reef at all, but a huge chain made of thousands of separate reefs.

This reef is home to an amazing amount of life. It has about four hundred kinds of coral and around fifteen hundred kinds of fish, plus thousands of types of shellfish. Sea turtles, sharks, and whales also visit or live in its waters.

Once a year, after a full moon in late spring, many corals on the reef spawn all at the same time. They release millions of tiny egg and sperm bundles into the water at night, and it looks like an underwater snowstorm going upward.

The reef is so important that it was named a World Heritage site by the United Nations in nineteen eighty one. It has been growing for a very long time, and scientists think the living part of today's reef began forming on older reef remains.

hook.en: Once a year, the whole reef spawns at once.

en: After plain water, tea is the most popular drink in the world. People drink billions of cups every day. Chinese legend says it was discovered about five thousand years ago, when a few leaves blew into the emperor's pot of boiling water.

True tea, whether it is green, black, white, or oolong, all comes from the very same plant, called Camellia sinensis. The difference is how the leaves are handled after picking. Herbal drinks made from flowers or fruit are not true tea at all.

The way people say the word tea shows how they once traded with China. Countries that bought tea by land, like Russia and Turkey, say chai, from the Chinese word cha. Countries that traded by sea, like England and the Netherlands, say tea.

The tea bag may have been a lucky accident. According to a popular story, around nineteen oh eight a New York tea seller mailed samples in little silk bags. Many customers dropped the whole bag into the cup, and a brand new way of making tea was born.

hook.en: The way you say tea reveals history.

en: There are far more trees on Earth than stars in our galaxy. A big study published in two thousand fifteen estimated about three trillion trees, while the Milky Way has somewhere between one hundred billion and four hundred billion stars.

A bristlecone pine in California called Methuselah is more than four thousand eight hundred years old. It was already growing when the pyramids of Egypt were being built, and it is still alive today. Its exact location is kept secret to protect it.

In Utah there is a forest that is really just one living thing. It is called Pando, a quaking aspen clone with about forty seven thousand trunks joined by one root system. It weighs an estimated six thousand tonnes, and scientists think it may be thousands of years old.

The tallest living tree known is a coast redwood in California named Hyperion. It stands about one hundred sixteen meters tall, taller than the Statue of Liberty from the ground to the tip of its torch, and it is thought to be six hundred to eight hundred years old.

hook.en: One forest in Utah is a single living thing.

en: Sloths move so slowly that algae actually grows in their fur. The algae gives their coat a greenish tint, which helps them blend into the leaves of the rainforest canopy. Some scientists think the algae may even give sloths a small snack.

A sloth spends almost its whole life in the trees, but about once a week it climbs all the way down to the ground to go to the bathroom. It digs a little hole, does its business, covers it up, and then slowly climbs back up.

Sloths are surprisingly good swimmers. They can paddle across rivers, and some reports say they can hold their breath underwater for up to forty minutes by slowing their heartbeat. On land they are slow, but in water they move much faster.

Long ago, giant ground sloths roamed the Americas. The biggest, called Megatherium, weighed about as much as an elephant, up to around four tonnes, and stood on its back legs to reach tree leaves. They died out roughly eleven thousand years ago.

hook.en: Sloths can hold their breath for forty minutes.

en: The tallest building in the world is the Burj Khalifa in Dubai. It reaches eight hundred twenty eight meters into the sky and has one hundred sixty three floors. It was completed in two thousand ten, and it took the record away from Taipei one oh one.

For almost four thousand years, the tallest human made structure was the Great Pyramid of Giza. It was only beaten around thirteen eleven, when the spire of Lincoln Cathedral in England rose higher. That is one of the longest world records in history.

Inside the skyscraper Taipei one oh one, a giant golden steel ball hangs between the eighty seventh and ninety second floors. It weighs about six hundred sixty tonnes. It swings gently the opposite way when wind or earthquakes shake the tower, keeping it steady.

When the Empire State Building opened in New York in nineteen thirty one, it became the tallest building in the world. It held that title for around forty years, until the towers of the World Trade Center rose higher in the early nineteen seventies.

hook.en: A giant golden ball protects a skyscraper.

en: The word alphabet comes from the first two letters of the Greek alphabet, alpha and beta. Those Greek names came from older Phoenician names. The first letter meant ox, and the second meant house, and that is why the letter A started out as a picture of an ox head.

Scientists think the very first alphabet appeared nearly four thousand years ago, around eighteen hundred before the common era. Workers who spoke a Semitic language in Egypt and the Sinai region borrowed a few Egyptian pictures and used them to stand for single sounds.

For a while in the nineteenth century, children learning the English alphabet recited twenty seven letters. The last one was the sign for the word and. Reciting it sounded like and per se and, and that is how the word ampersand was born.

Not every alphabet is long. The Rotokas language of Papua New Guinea has one of the shortest alphabets in the world, with only twelve letters. Meanwhile, the Cambodian alphabet is one of the longest in use, with more than seventy letters, so some languages need many more symbols than others.

hook.en: The English alphabet once had twenty seven letters.

en: Not every gladiator fight ended in death. Gladiators were expensive to train, so their owners did not want to lose them. A beaten fighter could ask for mercy, and the crowd and the organizer decided his fate. Many gladiators survived for years.

Some gladiators were free men who signed up on purpose. They gave up some of their rights in exchange for food, training, and a chance at fame and prize money. Many others were slaves or prisoners of war who had no choice at all.

Women fought as gladiators too. Roman writers mention them, and a carved stone from the ancient city of Halicarnassus is thought to show two female fighters. Emperor Septimius Severus is said to have banned women from the arena around the year two hundred.

Gladiators were nicknamed barley men, because they ate lots of barley and beans. Bone tests on gladiators buried in Ephesus show a mostly plant based diet. After fights, they may have drunk a drink made with plant ash, which could have helped their bones.

hook.en: Women fought as gladiators too.

en: Koalas sleep around twenty hours a day. Their food, eucalyptus leaves, gives very little energy and is poisonous to most animals, so koalas save energy by staying still. They wake up mostly at night to climb and eat a few hundred grams of leaves.

A koala is not a bear. It is a marsupial, which means the mother carries her baby in a pouch. A baby koala, called a joey, spends about six months inside the pouch, and its closest living relative is the wombat.

A koala has fingerprints that look almost exactly like human fingerprints. Even under a microscope, they can be very hard to tell apart. Besides primates, koalas are the only animals known to have such prints, and scientists think they help with gripping branches.

Baby koalas eat something strange. Around six or seven months old, the joey eats a soft food called pap from its mother. Pap carries the helpful gut bacteria that the baby will need to digest eucalyptus leaves for the rest of its life.

hook.en: Koala fingerprints look just like ours.

en: Your hands and feet are packed with bones. Each hand has twenty seven bones and each foot has twenty six. Add them up, and your two hands and two feet hold more than half of the two hundred and six bones in your whole adult skeleton.

Babies are born with kneecaps made of soft cartilage, not bone. Over the first years of childhood, usually somewhere between the ages of two and six, the cartilage slowly hardens into real bone, so very small children do not yet have a hard kneecap.

There is one bone in your body that is not connected to any other bone. It is a small U shaped bone in your throat called the hyoid. It floats in place, held only by muscles and ligaments, and it helps you swallow and speak.

Your skeleton is also a blood factory. Inside many of your bones is a soft tissue called marrow, and scientists estimate that it makes about two million new red blood cells every single second, replacing old ones that wear out.

hook.en: One bone in your body touches no other bone.

en: A day on Venus is longer than its year. Venus spins so slowly that one full turn takes about two hundred forty three Earth days, but the planet circles the Sun in only about two hundred twenty five Earth days. It is the only planet like this.

Venus spins backwards compared with most planets. If you could stand on its surface and see through the thick clouds, the Sun would rise in the west and set in the east, and the time from one sunrise to the next would be about four months.

Venus is the hottest planet in our solar system, even though Mercury is closer to the Sun. Its thick carbon dioxide air traps heat, so the surface stays at about four hundred sixty five degrees Celsius, hot enough to melt lead.

In nineteen eighty two, the Soviet probe Venera thirteen landed on Venus. The air pressure there is about ninety times stronger than on Earth, yet the little lander sent back color pictures and kept working for about two hours before it finally failed.

hook.en: Venus is hotter than Mercury.

en: Yawning starts before you are even born. Ultrasound scans show that babies in the womb begin to yawn when they are only about eleven weeks old, long before they can breathe air, see the world, or feel sleepy the way we do.

An average human yawn lasts around six seconds. Scientists who compared many animals found a pattern: species with bigger brains and more brain cells tend to have longer yawns, and humans were among the longest yawners in one big study.

Yawning is contagious. Seeing, hearing, or even reading about a yawn can make you yawn, and you probably just felt the urge. Scientists have also seen contagious yawning in some other animals, such as chimpanzees, and it may be linked to social bonds.

Nobody knows for sure why we yawn. It is not only about being sleepy, because people also yawn when bored. One popular idea is that a big yawn helps cool the brain, but scientists still argue about whether that is the real reason.

hook.en: You're probably about to yawn right now.

en: New York was once the capital of the United States. After the Constitution took effect, George Washington took his oath as the first president in New York City in seventeen eighty nine, standing on the balcony of Federal Hall on Wall Street.

The city began as a Dutch settlement called New Amsterdam, founded in sixteen twenty four. In sixteen sixty four the English took it over, without a big battle, and renamed it New York in honor of the king's brother, the Duke of York.

New York City may be the most linguistically diverse place on Earth. Researchers who map its languages say that more than seven hundred are spoken there, including some that are in danger of disappearing and have very few speakers left in the world.

Central Park is bigger than the whole country of Monaco. The park covers about eight hundred forty three acres, while Monaco covers about five hundred, and almost every hill, lake, and rock in the park was carefully designed and built by people.

hook.en: Over seven hundred languages are spoken in New York.

en: Ice floats, and that is very unusual. Most substances get denser when they freeze, but water expands by about nine percent as it turns into ice. That makes ice lighter than liquid water, so lakes freeze from the top and fish can survive below.

Ice cores from Antarctica are like time machines. Tiny bubbles trapped in the ice hold ancient air, and scientists have drilled a core with ice about eight hundred thousand years old, which shows them how our atmosphere and climate changed over time.

Ice has hidden forms. Scientists have found well over a dozen different crystal structures of ice, made by squeezing and cooling water. One rare kind, called ice seven, was even discovered trapped inside natural diamonds that formed deep inside the Earth.

Ice is slippery, but scientists are still debating exactly why. They agree that a very thin, watery layer on the surface makes it slick, but they do not agree on how that layer forms. The old idea of pressure melting is now thought to be too weak.

hook.en: There are more than a dozen kinds of ice.

en: Around fourteen fifty, a German goldsmith named Johannes Gutenberg built a printing press in the city of Mainz that used movable metal letters. Before that, almost every book in Europe had to be copied slowly by hand, one copy at a time.

Movable type was invented earlier in Asia. Chinese printers used movable clay type around the eleventh century, and a Korean book called Jikji, printed with metal type in thirteen seventy seven, is the oldest surviving book made that way, decades before Gutenberg was born.

The press spread very fast. By the year fifteen hundred, only about fifty years after Gutenberg, printing presses were working in around two hundred eighty cities across Europe, and millions of books had been printed, which helped ideas travel farther than ever before.

The words uppercase and lowercase come from printing. Printers kept capital letters in a case placed higher up and the small letters in a lower case, so the capitals became known as upper case letters. We still use these words on every keyboard.

hook.en: Printing spread across Europe in just fifty years.

en: Tides are caused mostly by the Moon. Its gravity pulls on the oceans and makes the water bulge on the side facing the Moon, and also on the opposite side, so most coasts get two high tides and two low tides every day.

The Bay of Fundy in Canada has the biggest tides in the world. At the biggest tides, the water in some places rises and falls by around sixteen meters, which is about the height of a five story building, in just a few hours.

The solid ground has tides too. The Moon and the Sun also pull on the Earth itself, so the land beneath your feet rises and falls by roughly twenty to thirty centimeters twice a day, and you never feel a thing.

Tides are slowly making our days longer. The friction of ocean tides slows down the spin of the Earth, and scientists measure that each day gets longer by about two milliseconds every hundred years. Days were shorter for the dinosaurs.

hook.en: The ground under your feet has tides too.

en: Hummingbirds are the only birds that can fly backwards. They can also hover in one place for a long time. Small species flap their wings around eighty times every second, and that super fast movement is what makes the humming sound you can hear.

A hummingbird has to eat almost all day. Its heart can beat more than one thousand times a minute while flying, and it drinks sugary nectar from hundreds of flowers daily, because it burns energy faster than almost any other warm blooded animal.

Hummingbirds can power down at night. When it is cold, they enter a deep sleep called torpor. Their heart rate and breathing drop sharply and their body cools down, which saves so much energy that they can survive until morning without any food.

The bee hummingbird of Cuba is the smallest bird in the world. It is only about six centimeters long and weighs about two grams, less than a small coin. Its nest is tiny too, roughly the size of a thimble.

hook.en: Hummingbirds almost shut down every night.

en: The oldest bread ever found is about fourteen thousand four hundred years old. Archaeologists discovered the burnt crumbs of flatbread in Jordan, left by hunter gatherers, which means people were baking bread more than four thousand years before they began farming wheat.

Bread rises because of tiny living things. Yeast is a single celled fungus that eats the sugar in dough and gives off carbon dioxide gas. The gas gets trapped in the stretchy dough, which puffs up and leaves the little holes inside every slice.

The people who built the great pyramids of Giza were paid in bread and beer. In ancient Egypt, grain was so important that bread and beer rations worked like a salary, and workers with higher status received bigger and better portions.

Sliced bread is less than a hundred years old. The first loaves of factory sliced bread were sold in nineteen twenty eight in Chillicothe, Missouri, using a machine invented by Otto Rohwedder. That is where the saying about the greatest thing since sliced bread comes from.

hook.en: The pyramid builders were paid in bread and beer.

en: As a young man, Julius Caesar was captured by pirates. According to ancient writers, he laughed when they asked for a ransom of twenty talents of silver and told them to ask for fifty. After he was freed, he returned with a fleet and caught them.

Caesar wrote his own war stories, and he wrote about himself as if he were someone else. In his famous book about the war in Gaul, he always says Caesar did this and Caesar did that, and he almost never says the word I.

The longest year in history was in forty six before the common era. When Caesar reformed the Roman calendar, the old calendar was so far off from the seasons that he added extra months, and that year lasted four hundred forty five days.

The month of July is named after Julius Caesar. It used to be called Quintilis, which means the fifth month, but after he was killed in forty four before the common era, the Romans renamed it in his honor. So every summer you say his name without even noticing it.

hook.en: One year in history lasted four hundred forty five days.

en: You have more than six hundred muscles in your body. Together they make up around forty percent of your body weight, and you use them for everything you do, from running a race to blinking, smiling, and even breathing while you sleep.

The largest muscle in your body is the gluteus maximus, in your buttocks, and the longest is the sartorius, which runs across your thigh. The smallest is the stapedius, a tiny muscle deep inside your ear that is only about a millimeter long.

Your tongue is not one muscle, it is a group of eight muscles woven together. It can move in almost every direction without a single bone inside to hold it up, and that is why it is so good at helping you speak and eat.

When you are cold, your muscles can heat you up. Shivering is your muscles contracting very fast, over and over, which makes heat. It is one of the ways your body tries to keep warm all by itself, without you even thinking about it.

hook.en: Your tongue is actually eight muscles.

en: Giant sequoias are the biggest trees on Earth by volume. The General Sherman Tree in California is about eighty four meters tall, and the National Park Service estimates it is around two thousand two hundred years old. Its trunk holds enough wood to build many houses.

Giant sequoias use fire to spread. Their cones can stay closed on the tree for years, and the heat of a forest fire dries them out so that they open and release thousands of seeds onto the bare, cleared soil below, where they can sprout.

Despite their enormous size, giant sequoias have shallow roots. The roots go down only about one or two meters, but they spread out far across the ground, over an area as wide as a football field, and tangle with the roots of nearby trees.

A giant sequoia comes with natural fire protection. The spongy bark can be up to about forty five centimeters thick and is full of a substance called tannin, so many old trees survive fires that would kill most other trees.

hook.en: The biggest trees have surprisingly shallow roots.

en: Uranus spins on its side. Its axis is tilted about ninety eight degrees, so it rolls around the Sun almost like a ball. Scientists think a giant collision long ago knocked the planet over, but they are still debating exactly what happened.

Because of that tilt, Uranus has the strangest seasons. Each pole gets about forty two years of constant sunlight followed by about forty two years of darkness, since one trip around the Sun takes the planet eighty four Earth years.

Scientists think the clouds of Uranus contain hydrogen sulfide, the gas that gives rotten eggs their smell. In twenty eighteen, astronomers using a telescope in Hawaii detected it, so if you could float in the upper air of Uranus, you would probably smell a terrible stink.

Uranus was the first planet discovered with a telescope. William Herschel spotted it in seventeen eighty one and at first thought it was a comet. He wanted to name it after the British king, George the Third, but astronomers later chose a name from Greek mythology instead.

hook.en: Uranus may smell like rotten eggs.

en: Sea otters have the thickest fur of any animal. They have up to about one million hairs in every square inch of skin, which traps air and keeps them warm, because unlike seals and whales they do not have a thick layer of blubber.

When sea otters rest, they often float together in groups called rafts, and some hold hands or wrap themselves in kelp so they do not drift apart while they sleep. Mothers also keep their pups close, often on their chests.

Sea otters have built in pockets. Under each front leg is a loose flap of skin where an otter can store food and even a favorite rock. They use that rock as a tool to crack open hard shells like clams and snails.

A sea otter must eat about a quarter of its body weight every day to stay warm. That means a heavy otter eats many kilograms of crabs, clams, and sea urchins daily, and it spends much of its day looking for food.

hook.en: Sea otters have built in pockets.

en: The Statue of Liberty was a gift from France to the United States, and it was dedicated on October twenty eighth, eighteen eighty six. It crossed the Atlantic Ocean in about three hundred fifty pieces, packed inside two hundred fourteen wooden crates.

The statue was not always green. It is made from thin copper sheets, each about as thick as two pennies, and at first it was a shiny reddish brown. Over about thirty years, air and rain slowly turned the copper green.

Hidden at the feet of Lady Liberty are broken chains and a broken shackle. Because of her long robe and how high she stands, they are hard to see from the ground, but they were meant to show freedom from oppression and slavery.

The pedestal almost was not built. The money ran out, so the newspaper publisher Joseph Pulitzer asked ordinary readers to help, and more than one hundred twenty thousand people donated, most of them giving less than one dollar each. Small gifts from ordinary people built the base.

hook.en: The Statue of Liberty hides broken chains.

en: Fire is not a thing, it is an event. It is the heat and light given off when fuel reacts quickly with oxygen. The glowing part of a flame is mostly hot gas and tiny bits of soot, heated until they shine.

Scientists think our ancestors were already using fire at least one million years ago. Burned bones and plant ash found deep inside Wonderwerk Cave in South Africa are some of the oldest signs of fire use by early humans, long before modern people existed.

Fire behaves very differently in space. Without gravity, hot air does not rise, so flames on the International Space Station form tiny blue balls instead of the tall yellow teardrops we see on Earth. They burn cooler and can even go out by themselves.

The matches we use today have a surprisingly recent history. In the eighteen twenties, an English chemist named John Walker was mixing chemicals with a stick. When he scraped a dried lump off the end, it burst into flame. He had accidentally invented the friction match, which people could strike anywhere.

hook.en: In space, fire burns in tiny blue balls.

en: Democracy was born in ancient Athens, around five hundred years before Christ. Citizens did not choose representatives, they voted directly on laws in a huge open air assembly. But only free adult men counted, so women and enslaved people had no vote at all.

The English word idiot comes from ancient Greek. An idiotes was a private person who stayed out of public life and politics. For the Greeks, ignoring the affairs of your city was considered foolish, and over time the word changed into an insult.

More than two thousand years ago, Greeks built a machine with gears. The Antikythera mechanism, found in a shipwreck in nineteen hundred and one, used bronze wheels to track the Moon, the Sun and eclipses. As far as we know, nothing this complex was built again for over a thousand years.

More than two thousand years ago, the Greek scholar Eratosthenes measured the size of the Earth. He compared the angle of the Sun's shadows in two different Egyptian cities and used simple geometry. His answer was surprisingly close to the true size of our planet.

hook.en: Ancient Greeks built a computer with gears.

en: Crows can recognize human faces, and they hold grudges. In a famous study, scientists wore a scary mask while catching crows. Years later, crows who had never been caught scolded anyone wearing that mask, so they must have learned it from other crows.

New Caledonian crows make and use tools in the wild. They snap twigs and bend them into hooks, and they shape leaves into little tools, to pull insects out of holes. Scientists have found that this clever tool use is a regular part of their lives in the forests of that Pacific island.

In Japan, wild crows have been filmed using traffic to crack nuts. They drop walnuts onto the road in front of cars, wait for the cars to drive over them, and then collect the broken pieces when the traffic light turns red and cars stop.

A group of crows is called a murder. Crows are also very social, and in winter thousands of them can gather to sleep together in one place. Crows belong to a family of clever birds that also includes ravens, magpies and jays.

hook.en: Crows use cars to crack their nuts.

en: The Nile and the Amazon have been arguing for years about which is the longest river. Both are around six thousand five hundred to seven thousand kilometers long. The answer depends on where you decide a river starts, and that is surprisingly hard to measure.

The Yangtze in China is the longest river in Asia, at about six thousand three hundred kilometers. It flows entirely inside one country, from glaciers high on the Tibetan plateau all the way to the East China Sea, near the huge city of Shanghai.

The Congo River in Africa is the deepest river in the world. In some places the water is more than two hundred meters deep, so deep that the bottom is completely dark. That is deeper than a sixty story building is tall.

The Nile flows north, which surprises many people, because we imagine rivers running down the map. It begins in the highlands near the equator and travels through eleven countries before reaching the Mediterranean Sea. Its water is shared by millions of people along the way.

hook.en: The deepest river in the world is in Africa.

en: The word okay began as a joke. In eighteen thirty nine, Boston newspapers loved funny misspellings, and one printed oh kay as a playful short form of the misspelled phrase all correct. It spread so widely that today almost every language on Earth knows it.

In London, Cockney rhyming slang hides words behind rhymes. Apples and pears means stairs, and dog and bone means phone. Often the rhyming part gets dropped, so only apples is left, and you need to know the code to understand.

The word dude is more than a century old, and it started as a joke at someone's expense. In eighteen eighties New York, a dude was an overdressed man who cared more about fashion than anything else. Over time it became a friendly word for anyone.

Slang changes so fast that dictionaries chase it. In twenty twenty three, Oxford University Press chose rizz as its word of the year. Dictionary experts believe it is a shortened form of the word charisma, and young people made it popular on the internet.

hook.en: The word dude started as a mockery.

en: Thomas Edison did not invent the first light bulb. Many inventors, including the Englishman Joseph Swan, had made lamps before him. Edison's success was building one that lasted long enough to sell, after testing thousands of materials for the thin glowing wire inside, even bamboo.

One light bulb in a fire station in Livermore, California, has been shining since nineteen oh one, according to Guinness World Records. It has gone dark only briefly, such as during a move in nineteen seventy six, and fans around the world watch it on a webcam.

In nineteen twenty four, the biggest light bulb makers around the world secretly agreed to limit how long their bulbs would last. They aimed for about one thousand hours, even though longer lasting bulbs could be made. Historians call this agreement the Phoebus cartel.

Old fashioned light bulbs are really tiny heaters. Only a small part of the electricity they use, roughly ten percent, becomes light, and the rest turns into heat. That is why a bulb of this kind is too hot to touch after it has been on for a while.
